subject: Financial Literacy
chapter: How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices
title: Ravi's Journey to the Stock Market
hook: When Ravi's father buys shares in India's biggest companies, he discovers how millions of Indians invest their money.

characters.name: Ravi
characters.role: Class 11 student from Mumbai discovering stock investing

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: Stock broker at a Mumbai brokerage firm

slides.title: How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices
slides.storyContext: Ravi and his grandfather visit the NSE (National Stock Exchange) office in Mumbai's financial district.

image.alt: How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices — How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices

slides.title: Setting the Scene
slides.storyContext: Ravi's grandfather, who invested ₹50,000 in Reliance Industries 20 years ago, now has ₹4 lakhs. At the NSE office, Ravi asks: 'Grandpa, how did your ₹50,000 become ₹4 lakhs? And what IS a stock anyway?' Priya, the broker, smiles: 'Let me show you how the stock market actually works—it's where buyers and sellers meet every second, deciding prices together.'

image.alt: Setting the Scene — How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices

slides.title: What Is a Stock?

points.label: Definition
points.text: A stock (or share) is a piece of ownership in a company. When you buy 1 share of TCS (Tata Consultancy Services), you own 1/(total shares) of that company.

points.label: Why Companies Issue Stocks
points.text: A company needs money to build factories, hire workers, buy machines. Instead of borrowing from a bank (and paying interest), they issue stocks to raise capital from the public.

points.label: What You Own
points.text: As a shareholder, you own a portion of the company's profits (via dividends), have voting rights in shareholder meetings, and can sell your share whenever you want.

example.problem: If Bajaj Auto issued 10 crore shares total, and you buy 100 shares, what fraction of Bajaj Auto do you own?
example.solution: You own 100 ÷ (10,00,00,000) = 0.000001% of Bajaj Auto. Not much individually, but millions of Indians own similar percentages—together, they own the entire company.

slides.inSimpleWords: A stock is like a piece of cake. If a company cuts itself into 10 crore equal pieces and sells them, you buying 100 pieces means you own a tiny part of that company forever (or until you sell it).

slides.title: How an IPO Works: TCS Goes Public
slides.storyContext: Priya explains: 'When TCS (Tata Consultancy Services) decided to go public in 1999, it was a private company owned by the Tata family. They needed capital to expand globally. So they issued 5 crore shares at ₹850 each, raising ₹4,250 crore. Today, TCS has ~42 crore shares, each worth ₹3400. That's a market cap of ₹14 lakh crore.'

example.problem: If TCS raised ₹4,250 crore at ₹850/share in 1999, how many shares did they sell?
example.solution: ₹4,250 crore ÷ ₹850 = 5 crore shares. These 5 crore shares went to public investors. The Tata Group retained ownership of some shares and also benefited from the ₹4,250 crore cash.

slides.inSimpleWords: An IPO (Initial Public Offering) is when a private company sells shares to the public for the first time. The company gets cash to grow; public investors get a piece of the company and hope for appreciation.

image.alt: How an IPO Works: TCS Goes Public — How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices

slides.title: The Market Opens: Millions Trading at Once
slides.storyContext: At 9:15 a.m., Priya shows Ravi the live trading screen at the NSE. Flashing red and green prices, numbers changing every second. 'Right now,' she says, 'over 1,000 traders are buying and selling Reliance. Some want to buy at ₹2649, some want to sell at ₹2650. When a buyer and seller agree, they trade instantly. The computer matches orders in microseconds. This happens millions of times per day across all 5,000 companies listed on NSE. That's how prices move.'

slides.title: The Stock Exchange: NSE and BSE

points.label: NSE (National Stock Exchange)
points.text: India's largest and most modern stock exchange, based in Mumbai. It handles ~₹10 lakh crore in daily trading volume. Most Class 11 students follow NSE indices.

points.label: BSE (Bombay Stock Exchange)
points.text: India's oldest stock exchange (founded 1875). Still active but smaller. Most companies are listed on both NSE and BSE simultaneously.

points.label: Why a Stock Exchange?
points.text: Without a central place, how would a buyer find a seller? The exchange creates a 'market' where millions of buyers and sellers meet via computer systems. It sets rules, ensures fair prices, and records every trade.

example.problem: At 10 a.m. on a Monday, a buyer wants to buy 1000 shares of HDFC Bank at any price. How does he find a seller?
example.solution: He logs into NSE via his brokerage app, places a buy order for 1000 HDFC shares. Within microseconds, the NSE's computer matches his order with a seller's sell order. If no seller at that price exists yet, his order waits in the 'order book' until someone sells at his price, or he raises his bid price.

slides.inSimpleWords: A stock exchange is like a huge farmer's market for company shares. Instead of shopkeepers calling out prices, computers match buyers and sellers instantly across the city.

image.alt: The Stock Exchange: NSE and BSE — How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices

slides.title: How Prices Are Set: Supply & Demand

points.label: Supply & Demand
points.text: If 1000 people want to buy Reliance shares (demand) but only 100 people want to sell (supply), the price rises. If 1000 want to sell and only 100 want to buy, the price falls.

points.label: Price Discovery
points.text: The stock price at any moment is the LAST price at which a buyer and seller agreed. It updates every second as new trades happen.

points.label: The Bid-Ask Spread
points.text: At any moment, there's a 'bid price' (highest price a buyer will pay RIGHT NOW) and an 'ask price' (lowest price a seller will accept RIGHT NOW). The spread between them is tiny for popular stocks like Reliance, wide for less-traded stocks.

example.problem: At 11:30 a.m., Reliance's bid price is ₹2649, ask price is ₹2650. A buyer buys 100 shares at ₹2650. What is the new 'last traded price'?
example.solution: ₹2650. The stock exchange updates the last traded price to ₹2650 instantly. This ₹2650 appears on every broker's app and every investor's screen. If the next buyer pays ₹2652, the last traded price becomes ₹2652.

slides.inSimpleWords: Stock prices move like a see-saw. When more people want to buy than sell, the price goes up. When more want to sell than buy, it goes down. Supply and demand decide the price—not the company or the government.

image.alt: How Prices Are Set: Supply & Demand — How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices

slides.title: Market Capitalization & Stock Splits

points.label: Market Cap (Market Capitalization)
points.text: Market Cap = Stock Price × Total Shares Outstanding. It's the total value investors are willing to pay for the entire company. Reliance's market cap is ~₹17 lakh crore (highest in India).

points.label: Why Market Cap Matters
points.text: A company with a ₹1000 crore market cap is 'smaller' (more risky, less established) than one with ₹1 lakh crore. Larger companies are often more stable.

points.label: Stock Splits
points.text: If a stock price gets very high (say ₹5000), it becomes hard for small investors to buy. Companies may split the stock 5:1 (each share becomes 5 shares at 1/5 the price). This doesn't change ownership %, just makes the price accessible.

example.problem: HDFC Bank's stock price is ₹2800, and there are 25 crore shares outstanding. What is HDFC Bank's market cap?
example.solution: Market Cap = ₹2800 × 25,00,00,000 = ₹7 lakh crore. If HDFC Bank announces a 5:1 stock split, each ₹2800 share becomes 5 shares at ₹560 each. The market cap stays ₹7 lakh crore—only the price per share changes.

slides.inSimpleWords: Market cap is the total price tag on a company. If a company is worth ₹1 lakh crore and has 10 crore shares, each share is worth ₹10,000. If they split 10:1, each share becomes ₹1000 but there are now 100 crore shares—the company's total value doesn't change.

image.alt: Market Capitalization & Stock Splits — How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices

slides.title: Ravi's First Trade
slides.storyContext: Priya helps Ravi open a demat account online. Within 10 minutes, Ravi is linked to NSE. Priya shows him: 'Look at Reliance's real-time chart. The price just jumped from ₹2649 to ₹2651 because news broke that Reliance signed a major energy deal. See how fast the market reacts? Thousands of traders are buying RIGHT NOW, pushing the price up. Sell orders are disappearing.' Ravi watches in awe as the price climbs to ₹2655 in seconds.

image.alt: Ravi's First Trade — How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices

slides.title: Order Types and Execution

points.label: Market Order
points.text: Buy or sell at the CURRENT market price immediately. If you place a market buy order for Reliance at 10:30 a.m., you get filled at whatever the ask price is at that instant (usually within ₹1-2 of the last price). Speed: instant.

points.label: Limit Order
points.text: Buy at a MAXIMUM price or sell at a MINIMUM price. You specify 'I'll buy Reliance only if it falls to ₹2640 or lower.' Your order waits in the order book until the price reaches ₹2640, then executes. Speed: when your limit is reached.

points.label: Stop Loss and Take Profit
points.text: Protective orders. Stop loss = 'sell if price falls to ₹2600 to limit my loss.' Take profit = 'sell if price rises to ₹2700 to lock in my gain.' Executes automatically at that price level.

example.problem: Ravi buys 100 Reliance shares at ₹2650 (market order, instantly executed). He immediately places a stop loss at ₹2600 and a take profit at ₹2750. What happens next?
example.solution: If Reliance falls to ₹2600, his stop loss triggers, and 100 shares are sold automatically at market price (roughly ₹2600), limiting his loss to ~₹5000. If Reliance rises to ₹2750, his take profit triggers, and 100 shares are sold, locking in his gain of ~₹10,000. He doesn't need to watch the screen all day—the orders protect him automatically.

slides.inSimpleWords: Market orders are 'buy now at any price.' Limit orders are 'buy ONLY if price hits this level.' Stop loss and take profit are automatic protective umbrellas—they sell for you if the stock falls too much (stop loss) or rises enough (take profit). Set them once, sleep easy.

image.alt: Order Types and Execution — How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices

slides.title: Trading vs. Investing: Risk and Time Horizon

points.label: Trading (Short-term, Days/Weeks)
points.text: Buy low, sell high within days or weeks. Traders chase quick price movements. High risk: you might buy at ₹2650 and panic-sell at ₹2600 if news turns negative. Plus brokerage fees, taxes (short-term capital gains taxed at 15–20%).

points.label: Investing (Long-term, Years/Decades)
points.text: Buy a good company and hold for 5–20 years. Investors ignore daily price swings and focus on company fundamentals (earnings growth, management quality). Lower taxes (long-term capital gains taxed at 10%+ slab is 20% with indexation benefit), lower stress.

points.label: Ravi's Grandfather's Strategy
points.text: He bought Reliance 20 years ago and held through recessions, crashes, and rallies. He didn't panic-sell during the 2008 crisis or the 2020 COVID crash. His patience turned ₹50,000 into ₹4 lakhs because Reliance's business grew and profits compounded.

example.problem: Ravi buys 100 Reliance at ₹2650 (investing goal). His friend Arjun buys 100 Reliance at ₹2650 (trading goal). Reliance falls to ₹2550 in 1 week. What happens?
example.solution: Arjun panics: 'I've lost ₹10,000 in 1 week! This is too risky.' He sells immediately, losing ₹10,000 + ₹500 in brokerage. Ravi doesn't flinch: 'Reliance is a solid company. A 3% dip is normal. I'll hold.' 6 months later, Reliance rises to ₹2900. Ravi gains ₹25,000 (and pays lower tax). Lesson: trading is stressful and expensive; investing is boring but profitable.

slides.inSimpleWords: Traders are like lightning bugs—quick, jittery, cash out fast. Investors are like trees—slow to grow, but they keep growing for decades. Grandpa Sharma is a tree. Reliance grew, and he grew with it.

image.alt: Trading vs. Investing: Risk and Time Horizon — How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices

slides.title: A Full Trading Day Example: Tata Steel
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma shows Ravi the 'Market Watch' on his phone, showing Tata Steel's trading throughout a day.

example.problem: On Day 1, Tata Steel opens at ₹130, hits a high of ₹135 (after good earnings news), a low of ₹128 (profit-taking), and closes at ₹133. Mr. Sharma bought 100 shares at ₹130 at market open. What is his gain/loss at close?
example.solution: Cost = 100 × ₹130 = ₹13,000. Market value at close = 100 × ₹133 = ₹13,300. Profit (on paper) = ₹13,300 − ₹13,000 = ₹300. But he hasn't sold yet, so this is an 'unrealised profit.' Only when he sells at ₹133 does it become real.

slides.inSimpleWords: Stock prices jump around during the day based on news, trading volume, and market sentiment. Your gains/losses are only real when you actually sell—until then, they're just paper gains.

image.alt: A Full Trading Day Example: Tata Steel — How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices

slides.title: Brokerage, Taxes, and Hidden Costs

points.label: Brokerage Fees
points.text: When you buy or sell a stock, your broker charges a commission (₹20–100 per trade or 0.01–0.05% of transaction value). Buying 100 shares at ₹2650: cost = ₹2,65,000 + ₹500 brokerage (approx). Selling later: same. Total cost: ₹1,000 in fees to make one round trip.

points.label: Short-term Capital Gains Tax (STCG)
points.text: If you sell within 1 year of buying, the profit is taxed as regular income: 15-30% slab depending on your income. Ravi (student) pays 0%; his father (30% slab) pays 30% tax on profits.

points.label: Long-term Capital Gains Tax (LTCG)
points.text: If you hold >1 year and sell, profits taxed at 20% (with indexation benefit) or 10% (without indexation). Much lower than STCG, so long-term investing saves you money on taxes.

example.problem: Ravi's father buys 100 Reliance at ₹2650, sells at ₹2750 after 6 months (short-term). Gain = ₹10,000. Brokerage = ₹500 (buying) + ₹500 (selling) = ₹1000. Net gain = ₹9,000. Tax at 30% (father's slab) = ₹2,700. Net after-tax profit = ₹9,000 − ₹2,700 = ₹6,300. What if he had held >1 year?
example.solution: Long-term gain = ₹10,000 − ₹1,000 (brokerage) = ₹9,000. Tax at 20% (LTCG) = ₹1,800. Net after-tax profit = ₹9,000 − ₹1,800 = ₹7,200. By holding 1 year longer, he keeps an extra ₹900 (tax saved)! This is why long-term investing beats trading for most investors.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every trade costs you money in brokerage and taxes. Trading frequently = bleeding money. Holding for years = keeping more money. Long-term investing is not only less stressful, it's also more profitable after taxes.

image.alt: Brokerage, Taxes, and Hidden Costs — How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices

slides.title: Mr. Sharma's Golden Rule
slides.storyContext: Ravi asks his grandfather: 'Grandpa, how do you stay calm when Reliance drops 10%? Shouldn't you sell immediately?' Mr. Sharma smiles and taps his chest: 'I invested in Reliance because I believe in its business model—refineries, petrochemicals, renewable energy, retail. The company fundamentals haven't changed. A 10% dip is just the market being moody. I buy more at lower prices. Over 20 years, I've bought Reliance at ₹800, ₹1200, ₹2000, ₹2500. On average, my cost is ₹1500 per share. Today, it's ₹2650. I'm patient. That's how wealth is built.'

image.alt: Mr. Sharma's Golden Rule — How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices

slides.title: Dividends and Rights Issues

points.label: Dividends
points.text: Profits that a company distributes to shareholders. If TCS earns ₹10,000 crore in profit and decides to distribute ₹4,000 crore as dividends (40% payout ratio), and you own 100 TCS shares, you receive cash equal to 100 × (₹4,000 crore ÷ total TCS shares). Quarterly or annually.

points.label: Dividend Yield
points.text: Annual dividend as a % of stock price. If TCS is ₹3400 and pays ₹85 per share annually, dividend yield = 2.5%. This is passive income just for holding the stock.

points.label: Rights Issues and Bonus Shares
points.text: Rights issue: company offers existing shareholders the right to buy NEW shares at a discount (e.g., 1 new share for every 5 held at ₹100, when market price is ₹120). Bonus: company gives free shares (e.g., 1 bonus for every 4 held). Both dilute price but reward patient shareholders.

example.problem: Ravi owns 100 Reliance shares at ₹2650. Reliance announces a 1:1 bonus (1 new share for each held, free) and quarterly dividend of ₹10 per share. What happens?
example.solution: Bonus: Ravi now owns 200 shares (doubled!), but price per share falls to ~₹1325 (to keep market cap constant). His total holding is still ₹265,000 market value. Dividend: 200 shares × ₹10 × 4 quarters = ₹8,000 per year in passive income. If Reliance's business grows, his 200 shares will eventually exceed ₹2650 again, and he'll be wealthier.

slides.inSimpleWords: Dividends are gifts from the company for being a shareholder. Free money while you sleep. Bonuses are more free shares. Companies reward patient, long-term investors with these perks.

image.alt: Dividends and Rights Issues — How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices

slides.title: Sectors and Diversification

points.label: Sectors in India
points.text: IT (TCS, Infosys, Wipro), Banking (HDFC, ICICI, Axis), Pharma (Sun Pharma, Cipla), Metals (Hindalco, JSW Steel), Auto (Maruti, Bajaj), FMCG (ITC, Britannia, Nestlé). Each sector responds differently to economic conditions.

points.label: Why Diversify
points.text: If you own only 10 Reliance shares, a bad oil price crash crashes your portfolio. But if you own Reliance (energy), TCS (IT), HDFC (banking), Sun Pharma (pharma), when energy crashes, IT and pharma might be stable or up. Diversification reduces risk.

points.label: Correlation and Uncorrelated Assets
points.text: Stocks in the same sector (two IT companies) tend to move together (high correlation). Stocks in different sectors (IT vs. Pharma) move independently (low correlation). A diversified portfolio has low correlation.

example.problem: Ravi has ₹50,000. Should he buy 200 Reliance shares (all energy) or diversify: 50 Reliance, 50 TCS, 50 HDFC, 50 ITC? What's the risk difference?
example.solution: All Reliance: if energy crashes (oil prices fall), all ₹50,000 is at risk. Diversified: if energy crashes, Reliance falls, but TCS (IT), HDFC (banking), ITC (FMCG) might stay stable. Diversification doesn't eliminate risk but spreads it. Ravi should diversify.

slides.inSimpleWords: Don't put all eggs in one basket. Own stocks from different industries so that if one industry struggles, others keep your portfolio afloat. A taxi driver with only Ola shares is highly risky. But Ola + Infosys + Cipla + Reliance = safer sleep.

image.alt: Sectors and Diversification — How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices

slides.title: When the Market Crashes: 2020 COVID Pandemic
slides.storyContext: Ravi watches the news: 'Sensex crashes 1000 points in one day!' He panics and calls his grandfather. Mr. Sharma calmly says: 'Ravi, this happened in 2008 (financial crisis), 2011 (European debt crisis), and now 2020 (COVID). Every time, investors panicked. Every time, patient investors bought more and became richer. The companies' businesses didn't disappear—only prices dropped. Fear makes prices irrational. This is when wealth is built, not lost. Don't sell; if you have cash, buy.' 6 months later, Reliance and TCS have recovered. Mr. Sharma's advice proved golden.

slides.title: Challenge: Calculate Your Own Profit
slides.storyContext: Ravi decides to invest his school project earnings. He buys 50 shares of ITC at ₹425 per share on Monday. On Friday, ITC is trading at ₹440. He also sees that ITC issued 10 crore shares and each share is worth ₹440.

points.text: Calculate Ravi's total investment.
Calculate the current market value of his 50 shares.
Calculate his unrealised profit.
What is ITC's approximate market cap if 10 crore shares × ₹440 = market cap?

example.problem: Answers:
example.solution: 1. Investment = 50 × ₹425 = ₹21,250. 2. Market value = 50 × ₹440 = ₹22,000. 3. Unrealised profit = ₹22,000 − ₹21,250 = ₹750 (or 3.5% return). 4. ITC's market cap ≈ 10,00,00,000 × ₹440 = ₹4.4 lakh crore.

image.alt: Challenge: Calculate Your Own Profit — How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices

slides.title: Challenge: Design Your Investment Strategy
slides.storyContext: Ravi has ₹50,000 saved. He wants to invest for 10 years. He asks Mr. Sharma for advice on how to build wealth in the stock market without losing sleep over daily price swings.

points.text: Should he invest all ₹50,000 at once or spread it over time? Why?
Which types of stocks should he pick—large-cap (Reliance, TCS, HDFC), mid-cap, or small-cap?
Should he use market orders or limit orders? Why?
What's his exit strategy—will he sell after 10 years, or hold longer? When?

example.problem: Strategy (from Mr. Sharma):
example.solution: 1. Spread over 10-12 months (₹4,000–5,000/month). This 'Systematic Investment Plan' (SIP) buys more shares when prices are low, fewer when high—reducing risk. 2. Pick large-cap stocks (80%)—Reliance, TCS, HDFC, Infosys, ITC. They're stable, pay dividends, less volatile. Add mid-caps (20%) for growth. 3. Use limit orders to avoid overpaying; patient investing means waiting for good entry prices. 4. Hold for 10 years minimum. If business is solid, hold 15-20 years. Sell only when you need money or fundamentals deteriorate. Discipline = wealth.

image.alt: Challenge: Design Your Investment Strategy — How the Stock Market Works — Buyers, Sellers & Prices

slides.title: Ravi's First Year: Patience Tested
slides.storyContext: A year later, Ravi's ITC shares have climbed to ₹460. He sees newspaper headlines: 'Market correction expected!' 'Analysts warn of overvaluation!' Friends urge him to sell. But Ravi remembers his grandfather's lesson. Instead of panicking, he buys 20 more ITC shares at ₹455 (lower price). Over the next 3 years, ITC grows to ₹650. His average cost is ₹435. His profit is now ₹7,750 on his total investment. He learns: buying on dips = wealth multiplication.

slides.title: What We Learned: Stock Market Basics

points.text: A stock is a piece of ownership in a company. Buying shares makes you a shareholder.
The NSE and BSE are stock exchanges where millions of buyers and sellers meet to trade stocks.
Stock prices are set by supply and demand—when more people want to buy, prices go up; when more want to sell, prices drop.
Market cap = Stock Price × Total Shares. It tells you the total value of a company.
Your profit is unrealised (on paper) until you actually sell. Mr. Sharma's ₹50,000 became ₹4 lakhs over 20 years because he held Reliance through ups and downs.
Trading (days/weeks) is risky and taxed heavily. Investing (years/decades) is boring but profitable and tax-efficient. Patience builds wealth.

slides.inSimpleWords: The stock market is where you can own tiny pieces of big Indian companies. Prices change every second based on what buyers and sellers decide—and your wealth grows slowly if you invest in good companies and hold them long-term.

subject: Financial Literacy
chapter: Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices
title: Priya's Guide to Market Indices
hook: Every morning, Priya checks the Sensex and Nifty on her phone. Are they up or down? What do they really mean for her investments?

characters.name: Priya
characters.role: Young investor and financial analyst in Mumbai

characters.name: Amit
characters.role: Priya's friend who trades using index funds

slides.title: Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices
slides.storyContext: Priya sits with her mentor Mr. Kapoor at a coffee shop near the BSE building in Mumbai. 'I see Sensex up 500 points today,' she says, 'but I don't understand what it means for my portfolio.'

image.alt: Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices — Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices

slides.title: The Confusion Behind the Headlines
slides.storyContext: 'Every news channel shouts—Sensex is up! Nifty is down! But Priya, this confuses most people,' Mr. Kapoor explains. 'An index isn't a stock you can buy. It's a snapshot—a scoreboard showing how India's biggest companies are doing together. Think of it as the health report of the entire stock market.' He pulls up his phone: 'The Sensex shows 30 companies. The Nifty shows 50. These two indices tell us if the market is moving up or down—and how badly your investments might swing.'

image.alt: The Confusion Behind the Headlines — Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices

slides.title: What Is a Market Index?

points.label: Definition
points.text: A market index is a weighted average of selected stocks. It's a number (like 72,000 for Sensex) that represents the collective price movement of those stocks.

points.label: Why Indices Exist
points.text: With 5,000+ stocks listed in India, it's impossible to track every one. Indices pick the biggest, most-traded companies to show the 'direction' of the market. If Sensex is up, it usually means large-cap Indian companies are doing well.

points.label: Not Directly Investable
points.text: You CANNOT buy 'the Sensex' itself. But you can buy a Sensex Index Fund, which holds all 30 Sensex stocks in the same proportion. Your money then moves with the Sensex.

example.problem: Imagine an 'index' of just 3 stocks: Stock A at ₹100, Stock B at ₹200, Stock C at ₹300. The index value = (100 + 200 + 300) ÷ 3 = 200. Next day: A goes to ₹120, B to ₹220, C to ₹280. What is the new index value?
example.solution: New index = (120 + 220 + 280) ÷ 3 = 206.67. The index went up from 200 to 206.67. So we'd say 'the index rose 6.67 points' or about 3.3%. Even though Stock C fell, the index rose because A and B rose more.

slides.inSimpleWords: An index is like a group report card for major companies. Instead of looking at 100 report cards, you peek at the top 30 (Sensex) or top 50 (Nifty). If the group score goes up, the market is happy. If it goes down, investors are worried.

slides.title: The BSE Sensex: India's Flagship Index

points.label: Full Name
points.text: S&P BSE SENSEX (Bombay Stock Exchange's Sensitive Index). Launched in 1986 with a base index value of 100.

points.label: Composition
points.text: 30 largest, most-traded stocks from the BSE. These represent ~40-45% of the market's total value. Companies like Reliance, TCS, HDFC, Infosys, ITC, Bajaj Auto are always in the Sensex.

points.label: Weighted by Market Cap
points.text: Larger companies (higher market cap) have more weight. Reliance, with a ₹17 lakh crore market cap, affects the Sensex more than a ₹1 lakh crore company would. When Reliance rises 5%, the Sensex typically rises ~1-2%.

points.label: Benchmark for India's Economy
points.text: The Sensex is THE barometer of India's economic health. If Sensex rises 10% in a year, investors believe India's top companies are thriving.

example.problem: On Monday, the Sensex closes at 70,000. On Tuesday, news arrives that Reliance (25% of Sensex weight) will miss its profit target. Reliance stock falls 8%. Roughly how much will the Sensex fall?
example.solution: Reliance's 8% fall × 25% weight = approximately 2% of the Sensex's move. So Sensex might fall roughly 1,400 points (2% of 70,000). However, other stocks might move up or down, so the actual fall could be 1000–1800 points depending on the rest of the market.

slides.inSimpleWords: The Sensex is like the pulse of India Inc. It measures the 30 biggest companies. If Reliance (the heaviest company) coughs, the whole Sensex feels it. That's why news about Reliance moves the Sensex more than news about a smaller company.

image.alt: The BSE Sensex: India's Flagship Index — Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices

slides.title: The NSE Nifty: The Modern Index

points.label: Full Name
points.text: NIFTY 50 (National Stock Exchange's 50 stocks). Launched in 1996 and is now India's primary index for derivatives and index funds.

points.label: Composition
points.text: 50 largest stocks across sectors: IT (TCS, Infosys, Wipro), Banks (HDFC, ICICI, Axis), Auto (Maruti, Bajaj), Pharma (Sun Pharma), Metals (Hindalco).

points.label: Why Nifty Over Sensex?
points.text: Nifty includes 50 stocks (vs. Sensex's 30), so it's more representative of the entire market. It's also hosted on NSE, which is more modern and liquid. Nifty is the standard for index funds and algo trading.

points.label: Nifty Variants
points.text: Nifty 100 (100 stocks), Nifty 200 (200 stocks), Nifty Next 50 (51–100 market cap). Each serves a different purpose.

example.problem: Amit invests ₹1,00,000 in a Nifty 50 Index Fund. The fund holds all 50 Nifty stocks in the same proportion as the Nifty index. On Day 1, Nifty is at 20,000. On Day 2, Nifty closes at 20,400 (up 2%). Approximately how much is Amit's fund worth now?
example.solution: If Nifty rose 2%, Amit's fund should also rise roughly 2% (minus tiny fund fees, ~0.1%–0.3% annually). So his fund ≈ ₹1,00,000 × 1.02 = ₹1,02,000. He gained ₹2000 (on paper) because the 50 companies in Nifty collectively rose 2%.

slides.inSimpleWords: Nifty is like the Sensex's younger, smarter sibling. It tracks 50 companies instead of 30, so it's a clearer picture of India's market. Most new investors track Nifty because it's more balanced.

image.alt: The NSE Nifty: The Modern Index — Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices

slides.title: Priya Reads the Morning Headlines
slides.storyContext: Priya opens her financial news app at 9:30 a.m. (market opens). Headlines read: 'Sensex up 350 points!' 'RBI Rate Cut Boosts Markets!' 'Rupee Weakens Against Dollar.' Mr. Kapoor points out: 'Now you must ask: Why are the indices up? Is it driven by overall economic optimism (everyone up) or just a few heavyweight stocks? Are smaller stocks also rallying or falling? This context matters more than the headline number.'

image.alt: Priya Reads the Morning Headlines — Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices

slides.title: Reading a Stock's Data: P/E, Dividend, Volume

points.label: P/E Ratio (Price-to-Earnings)
points.text: P/E = Stock Price ÷ Earnings Per Share (EPS). If a stock is ₹100 and EPS is ₹10, P/E = 10. It tells you how many rupees investors pay for every rupee of profit the company earns. High P/E = market expects growth; Low P/E = stock might be undervalued (or risky).

points.label: Dividend Yield
points.text: Dividend = yearly cash payout per share. If a stock is ₹1000 and annual dividend is ₹50, yield = 5%. You earn ₹50 per share per year just by holding it (until you sell). Not all companies pay dividends.

points.label: Volume
points.text: How many shares were traded in a day. High volume = liquid (easy to buy/sell without moving the price much). Low volume = hard to find a buyer/seller, price might swing wildly. For Reliance, daily volume is ~3 crore shares; for a small stock, maybe 1 lakh shares.

example.problem: You're comparing two stocks: Stock A (₹500, P/E = 20, Dividend = 3%) vs. Stock B (₹500, P/E = 10, Dividend = 0%). Which is 'cheaper'? Which is safer?
example.solution: Stock B is cheaper (P/E 10 vs. 20)—you pay ₹10 for every ₹1 of profit vs. ₹20 for Stock A. But it pays no dividend. Stock A expects faster growth (why investors pay a higher P/E). Stock A is safer for income investors; Stock B is riskier but might appreciate faster. Neither is objectively 'better'—it depends on your goals.

slides.inSimpleWords: When you see a stock quote (Reliance: ₹2650, P/E: 22, Dividend: 2.3%), you're reading the company's financial report card. P/E tells you if it's expensive or cheap. Dividend tells you if it pays you cash to hold it. Volume tells you if you can easily buy or sell.

image.alt: Reading a Stock's Data: P/E, Dividend, Volume — Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices

slides.title: Market Breadth and Advance-Decline Ratio

points.label: Market Breadth
points.text: Number of stocks that rose (Advances) vs. fell (Declines) on a given day. If Advances = 1,800 and Declines = 1,200, it's a bullish day (most stocks rising). If Declines > Advances, it's bearish (most stocks falling).

points.label: Advance-Decline Line
points.text: A cumulative measure of (Advances − Declines) over weeks/months. If A-D line is rising steeply, market has 'internal strength'—many stocks are rallying, not just the top 50. If A-D line is flat while indices are rising, it signals 'narrow market'—only big stocks are up (warning sign).

points.label: Why It Matters
points.text: Indices can be misleading. Sensex up 2% but Declines > Advances means the big-cap stocks are artificially pumping the index while the broader market is weak. Smart investors use breadth to validate (or question) index strength.

example.problem: On Tuesday: Sensex up 500 points (0.7%). Nifty up 200 points (0.95%). Advances = 1,200, Declines = 1,600. Is this a true rally or a trap?
example.solution: Trap! Declines (1,600) > Advances (1,200). Most stocks are falling, but the indices are up because Reliance, TCS, HDFC (super heavy-weight) are rallying. The broader market (small/mid-caps) is weak. A smart investor would be cautious and wait for breadth to improve before buying big.

slides.inSimpleWords: If Sensex rises 2% but most stocks fall, something's wrong. It's like a class of 100 students where 60 fail, but the top 5 genius students do so well that the class average is a pass. That average doesn't reflect reality. Real strength = most stocks rising.

image.alt: Market Breadth and Advance-Decline Ratio — Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices

slides.title: Reading the Morning Market Report: A Real Example
slides.storyContext: Priya opens her broker app at 9:20 a.m. (right after market opens). She sees this snapshot.

example.problem: Snapshot: Sensex 70,500 (up 300 points, +0.43%). Nifty 21,100 (up 80 points, +0.38%). Reliance ₹2650 (down 0.5%). TCS ₹3400 (up 1.2%). Market Breadth: Advances 1850, Declines 1420, Unchanged 120. Amit says, 'Market is up, but Reliance is down—is something wrong with Reliance?' What should Priya tell him?
example.solution: No, it's normal. Even when the overall market (Sensex, Nifty) is up, individual stocks can move differently. Reliance fell 0.5% (perhaps profit-taking or some news), while TCS rose 1.2% (maybe good quarterly results). The 'Advances 1850, Declines 1420' means 1850 stocks rose and 1420 fell—so the market is slightly bullish. Reliance is just lagging today.

slides.inSimpleWords: The Sensex and Nifty are UP, but your individual stock might be DOWN. They're separate stories. The index shows the overall mood of the market; individual stocks are affected by company-specific news (earnings, management changes, scandals, etc.). Always read both the index AND your stock separately.

image.alt: Reading the Morning Market Report: A Real Example — Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices

slides.title: Bullish and Bearish Signals: Technical vs. Fundamental

points.label: Bullish Signals
points.text: Indices up, volume high, breadth strong, corporate earnings growing. Or: interest rates cut, rupee stable, FDI inflows. Or: technical: Nifty above its 200-day moving average, support levels holding.

points.label: Bearish Signals
points.text: Indices down on high volume, breadth weak, earnings misses, unemployment rising. Or: interest rates rising, rupee weakening, foreign investor selling. Or: technical: Nifty below 50-day moving average, broken support.

points.label: Sentiment vs. Reality
points.text: Markets are driven by SENTIMENT (fear/greed) as much as fundamentals. In 2020 COVID crash, Sensex fell 40%, but India's businesses didn't collapse—sentiment did. Investors panicked, sold everything. This is why lows are buying opportunities.

example.problem: March 2020: Sensex crashes from 42,000 to 25,600 (39% fall) in weeks due to COVID lockdown panic. Reliance, TCS, HDFC—all solid companies—fell 30–40%. By Dec 2020, all stocks rebounded 80%+. What happened?
example.solution: Sentiment crashed in March (people feared 'end of the world'). But reality didn't change much—India's core businesses, government, tax base were intact. By Dec, fear eased, investors returned, and prices rebounded. This teaches: big corrections are usually emotional, not fundamental. Patient investors who bought in April-June 2020 became very wealthy by 2022-23.

slides.inSimpleWords: Markets swing between panic (crash) and euphoria (rally). Smart investors buy during panic and sell during euphoria. The companies' actual businesses change slowly; the prices change fast. This mismatch is where wealth is made.

image.alt: Bullish and Bearish Signals: Technical vs. Fundamental — Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices

slides.title: Priya Tracks the Index for a Month
slides.storyContext: Priya creates a simple spreadsheet: every day, she records the Sensex opening, closing, volume, breadth, and top movers. After 4 weeks: 'Mr. Kapoor, I notice Sensex rose 2% (bullish), but half the days had Declines > Advances. What's that mean?' Mr. Kapoor smiles: 'You spotted a 'narrow rally'—big stocks are carrying the market while mid/small-caps are suffering. This isn't sustainable. When the rally broadens, even small stocks rise—that's a sign of healthy bull market. Right now, the market is fragile.'

slides.title: Priya's Learning: Index Funds vs. Stock Picking
slides.storyContext: After 3 months of trying to pick individual stocks (and underperforming), Priya sits with Mr. Kapoor again. 'I've been reading every company quarterly report, tracking P/E ratios, but my portfolio is up only 2% while Nifty is up 5%.' Mr. Kapoor smiles: 'This is the most important lesson for a Class 11 student. Even professionals struggle to beat the index. Most of them don't. So why not just buy a Nifty 50 Index Fund, match the market returns, and spend time on your studies or side businesses instead?' Priya nods: 'So you're saying I should give up on investing?' 'No,' Mr. Kapoor says, 'invest regularly in index funds for the base wealth. Then, for 10-20% of your portfolio, stock-pick to learn and chase outsized gains. Balance, not all-or-nothing.'

image.alt: Priya's Learning: Index Funds vs. Stock Picking — Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices

slides.title: Sector-Specific Indices: Banking, IT, Pharma

points.label: Nifty Bank Index
points.text: 12 major banks (HDFC, ICICI, Axis, SBI, etc.). Moves based on RBI interest rate decisions, loan growth, NPA (bad loans).

points.label: Nifty IT Index
points.text: Major IT companies (TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCL). Moves based on dollar rates, US tech spending, offshore earnings.

points.label: Nifty Pharma Index
points.text: Pharmaceutical companies (Sun Pharma, Cipla, Lupin). Moves based on drug price regulations, drug approvals, forex.

example.problem: On a day when the overall Nifty 50 is flat (0% change), Nifty Bank rises 2% and Nifty IT falls 1.5%. Why might this happen?
example.solution: RBI might have cut interest rates (good for banks, as they can lend more easily), while rupee weakness (bad for IT, as they earn in dollars but spend in rupees). Sector-specific indices show that different industries respond differently to the same economic news.

slides.inSimpleWords: Different sectors rise and fall at different times. When oil prices rise, energy stocks soar but airlines crash. When rupee weakens, IT stocks suffer but pharma export profits rise. Smart investors track sector indices to spot these patterns.

slides.title: Challenge: Analyze a Market Day
slides.storyContext:
On a Tuesday, you see this in the newspaper:
—Sensex: 71,200 (up 700, +0.99%)
—Nifty 50: 21,300 (up 200, +0.95%)
—Top gainers: Maruti (+3.5%), Bajaj Auto (+2.8%)
—Top losers: Asian Paints (−2.1%), Nestle (−1.5%)
—Market Volume: Highest in 3 months

Questions: 1. Is this a 'bullish' or 'bearish' day? 2. Why might auto stocks rally while consumer stocks fall? 3. If you own only Asian Paints, did you have a good day?

example.problem: Answers:
example.solution: 1. Bullish day—Sensex up nearly 1%, and volume is high (shows conviction). 2. Auto stocks rallied possibly due to good sales data or lower raw material costs; consumer stocks fell possibly due to inflation concerns or earnings misses. 3. No—if the market rose 1% but your Asian Paints fell 2.1%, you underperformed by 3.1% relative to the market. This happens when individual companies face company-specific headwinds while the broader market is strong.

image.alt: Challenge: Analyze a Market Day — Reading Stocks — Sensex, Nifty & Market Indices

slides.title: Challenge: Build Your Own Index Tracking
slides.storyContext: Priya decides to create a simple '5-stock mini index' with her friends' favorite companies: TCS (30% weight), Reliance (25%), HDFC (20%), ITC (15%), Maruti (10%). If these stocks move as follows in one day: TCS +1.5%, Reliance −0.5%, HDFC +0.8%, ITC +1.2%, Maruti −1%, what is the mini index's return?

points.text: Calculate TCS's contribution: 1.5% × 30%
Calculate Reliance's contribution: −0.5% × 25%
Calculate HDFC's contribution: 0.8% × 20%
Calculate ITC's contribution: 1.2% × 15%
Calculate Maruti's contribution: −1% × 10%

example.problem: Answers (contributions):
example.solution: TCS: 0.45%; Reliance: −0.125%; HDFC: 0.16%; ITC: 0.18%; Maruti: −0.10%. Sum = 0.45 − 0.125 + 0.16 + 0.18 − 0.10 = 0.565% or ~0.57% gain. So your 'mini index' rose 0.57%. This is how the Sensex and Nifty calculations work—each stock's move is weighted by its market cap.

slides.title: What We Learned: Reading the Market

points.text: A market index is a weighted average of selected stocks. Sensex (30 stocks) and Nifty 50 (50 stocks) are India's main indices.
You cannot buy 'the Sensex' directly, but you can buy a Sensex/Nifty Index Fund that mirrors it.
The Sensex and Nifty move together most days, but individual stocks can diverge. Always read both.
P/E ratio tells you if a stock is 'expensive' or 'cheap.' Dividend yield tells you annual cash payout. Volume tells you liquidity.
Market Breadth (Advances vs. Declines) shows the overall market mood. High volume + index up = bullish; high volume + index down = bearish; low volume = indecision.
Markets are driven by sentiment (fear/greed) as much as fundamentals. Big crashes are usually buying opportunities; euphoria rallies are time to be cautious.

slides.inSimpleWords: The Sensex and Nifty are scorecards for India Inc. They move with the big companies. But individual stocks have their own stories. A smart investor reads BOTH—the overall market AND their own holdings.

subject: Financial Literacy
chapter: Bonds, FDs & Fixed Income — Lending Your Money
title: Akshay's Quest for Safe Returns
hook: Akshay has ₹10 lakhs. Stocks are exciting but risky. Can he lend money to the government or a bank and earn interest safely?

characters.name: Ms. Gupta
characters.role: Bank manager helping Akshay understand fixed-income products

slides.title: Bonds, FDs & Fixed Income — Lending Your Money
slides.storyContext: Akshay visits his bank in Delhi after receiving ₹10 lakhs from his grandfather's estate. 'I don't want to lose this money in the stock market,' he tells Ms. Gupta. 'Can I earn interest safely?' Ms. Gupta smiles: 'Yes. You can lend your money to the government or the bank. That's fixed income.'

image.alt: Bonds, FDs & Fixed Income — Lending Your Money — Bonds, FDs & Fixed Income — Lending Your Money

slides.title: The Safety vs. Returns Dilemma
slides.storyContext: 'Stocks give high returns but are risky,' Rahul explains to Akshay. 'Bonds and FDs give lower returns but are much safer because you are lending money, not buying ownership. If Reliance stock goes to zero, you lose everything. But if you lend money to the government in a 10-year bond, the government MUST pay you back—they have the entire nation's tax revenue to back it.' Akshay nods: 'So I trade higher returns for safety?' Rahul: 'Exactly. High-school Akshay won't get rich quick from FDs. But in 20 years, a steady stream of FDs will build solid wealth.'

image.alt: The Safety vs. Returns Dilemma — Bonds, FDs & Fixed Income — Lending Your Money

slides.title: What Is a Bond?

points.label: Definition
points.text: A bond is a debt instrument. When you buy a bond, you lend money to a government or corporation for a fixed period (e.g., 10 years). In return, they pay you interest (called 'coupon') periodically and return your principal at maturity.

points.label: Bond Issuer
points.text: Governments issue bonds to fund infrastructure (roads, schools). Corporations issue bonds to fund expansion. If you buy a Government Security (G-Sec), you are lending to the Indian government.

points.label: Key Terms
points.text: Face Value = principal (e.g., ₹1000 per bond). Coupon Rate = annual interest rate (e.g., 6% per year). Maturity = when you get your money back (e.g., 10 years). If you hold to maturity, you're guaranteed your principal + all coupons.

example.problem: Akshay buys a 10-year Government Bond with a face value of ₹1,00,000 and coupon rate of 6%. How much interest will he earn per year? How much total will he receive over 10 years?
example.solution: Annual interest = ₹1,00,000 × 6% = ₹6,000 per year. Over 10 years: ₹6,000 × 10 = ₹60,000 in coupons. At maturity (year 10), he gets back ₹1,00,000 principal. Total received = ₹60,000 (coupons) + ₹1,00,000 (principal) = ₹1,60,000.

slides.inSimpleWords: A bond is a formal 'IOU' between you and a borrower. You lend ₹1,00,000 to the government at 6% interest for 10 years. Every year, the government sends you ₹6,000. After 10 years, you get your ₹1,00,000 back. No surprises—if the government doesn't pay, it's a huge scandal (rarely happens with Indian G-Secs).

image.alt: What Is a Bond? — Bonds, FDs & Fixed Income — Lending Your Money

slides.title: Fixed Deposits (FDs) and Certificate of Deposits (CDs)

points.label: Fixed Deposit (FD)
points.text: You deposit money in a bank for a fixed period (7 days to 10 years). The bank pays you a fixed interest rate. After the period, you withdraw your money + interest. FDs are issued by banks and are INSURED by DICGC up to ₹5 lakhs per bank per customer.

points.label: FD Interest Rates
points.text: Banks typically offer 3–7% interest depending on tenure. Longer tenures have higher rates (bank locks your money longer, so it pays you more). Shorter tenures have lower rates (but you can reinvest quickly).

points.label: Certificate of Deposit (CD)
points.text: Similar to FD, but issued by corporations (not banks). CDs offer slightly higher rates (5–8%) because corporations are riskier than banks. But they are NOT INSURED (if the corporation defaults, you lose money).

points.label: Tax on FD Interest
points.text: If you earn interest >₹40,000/year, you must pay tax. FD interest is added to your annual income and taxed at your slab (for Class 11 student Akshay at 0% tax slab, FD interest is tax-free; for his father at 30% slab, it's taxed at 30%).

example.problem: Akshay deposits ₹5 lakhs in a bank FD at 6.5% per annum for 3 years. How much will he have at maturity? What if he had chosen a CD at 7.5% from a reputable corporation?
example.solution: FD: ₹5,00,000 × 6.5% × 3 = ₹97,500 interest (simple interest, though some FDs offer compound interest). Total = ₹5,97,500. CD (7.5%): ₹5,00,000 × 7.5% × 3 = ₹1,12,500 interest. Total = ₹6,12,500. But the CD is risky—if the corporation defaults, Akshay gets nothing. The FD is safer because it's bank-backed and insured up to ₹5 lakhs.

slides.inSimpleWords: An FD is like giving your money to the bank with a promise: 'Keep this for 3 years, and I'll pay you 6.5% interest annually.' The bank guarantees to return your money + interest at the end. CDs work similarly but with corporations instead of banks—and they're riskier.

image.alt: Fixed Deposits (FDs) and Certificate of Deposits (CDs) — Bonds, FDs & Fixed Income — Lending Your Money

slides.title: Government Securities (G-Secs) and Savings Schemes

points.label: Government Securities (G-Secs)
points.text: Bonds issued by the Government of India. T-Bills (short-term, <1 year), T-Bonds (medium-term, 2–10 years), and T-Notes (long-term, 10–40 years). Interest rates depend on tenure: longer bonds typically pay more interest.

points.label: National Savings Certificates (NSC)
points.text: Savings scheme where you deposit money and get a fixed return (currently ~8% compounded semi-annually) for 5 or 10 years. No tax on interest earned (tax-free benefit)! Maximum ₹1.5 lakhs per person per year.

points.label: Public Provident Fund (PPF)
points.text: Long-term savings scheme (15-year tenure with optional extension). Interest rate ~7.1% (reviewed quarterly). Maximum ₹1.5 lakhs contribution per year. Primarily for retirement but can withdraw partially after 7 years. Tax-free!

points.label: Post Office Savings Schemes
points.text: Senior Citizen Savings Scheme (10 years, ~8.2%), Sukanya Samriddhi Yojana (21 years for girls, tax-free), etc. All are safe because they're backed by the government.

example.problem: Akshay invests ₹1.5 lakhs in NSC (8% p.a., compounded semi-annually) for 5 years. How much will he have at maturity?
example.solution: Compound formula: A = P(1 + r/2)^(2n) where P = ₹1,50,000, r = 8%, n = 5 years. A = 1,50,000 × (1.04)^10 = 1,50,000 × 1.4802 = ₹2,22,027 (approximately). He gains ₹72,027 in interest, TAX-FREE. No TDS, no tax on withdrawal.

slides.inSimpleWords: Government savings schemes (NSC, PPF, G-Secs) are like giving your money to India's government. They promise you steady, guaranteed returns (7–8%) and most are tax-free. They're the safest investments because if the government goes broke, the entire nation goes broke.

image.alt: Government Securities (G-Secs) and Savings Schemes — Bonds, FDs & Fixed Income — Lending Your Money

slides.title: Akshay Discovers Compound Interest
slides.storyContext: Rahul shows Akshay a chart: 'If you invest ₹10 lakhs in PPF at 7.1% p.a. for 15 years, how much will you have?' Akshay thinks: '7.1% × 15 = 106.5%, so ₹10L × 2.065 = ₹20.65 lakhs?' Rahul smiles and pulls out his calculator: 'No. Compound interest is not linear. A = 10L × (1.071)^15 = ₹27.86 lakhs. See? Compound interest added ₹7.86 lakhs extra!' Akshay's jaw drops: 'That's ₹7.86 lakhs I earned just by waiting 15 years without doing anything!' Rahul nods: 'Exactly. Einstein called it the 8th wonder of the world. Time + compound interest = wealth without effort.'

image.alt: Akshay Discovers Compound Interest — Bonds, FDs & Fixed Income — Lending Your Money

slides.title: Bond Prices, Yields, and Duration

points.label: Bond Price vs. Coupon
points.text: If you buy a bond at issuance at face value (say ₹1000, 6% coupon), and interest rates rise to 8%, new bonds paying 8% become attractive. Your 6% bond becomes less desirable—its price in the secondary market falls below ₹1000 (say ₹950). If rates fall to 4%, your 6% bond becomes attractive—its price rises above ₹1000 (say ₹1050).

points.label: Yield to Maturity (YTM)
points.text: If you buy a bond at a discount (below face value) and hold it to maturity, your actual annual return is the YTM, NOT just the coupon rate. A bond bought at ₹950 with ₹60 annual coupon has a different YTM than face value.

points.label: Duration
points.text: How long until you get your money back (weighted by cash flows). A 10-year bond has higher duration risk than a 1-year bond. If you need money in 2 years but hold a 10-year bond, you must sell early (risking loss if rates rose).

example.problem: You buy a bond at face value ₹1000, coupon 6%, maturity 10 years. Interest rates rise, and the bond's market price falls to ₹900. If you sell now, you lose ₹100. But if you hold to maturity, you get ₹1000 back. What is the lesson?
example.solution: If you HOLD bonds to maturity, you're guaranteed face value. You don't need to worry about price fluctuations. But if you SELL before maturity, you might incur a loss (or gain if rates fell and price rose). Akshay, holding to maturity, avoids this risk—he gets ₹1000 + all coupons no matter what.

slides.inSimpleWords: Bond prices swing like stocks if you sell early. But if you hold to maturity, you're guaranteed your principal + all interest payments. The risk of bond prices falling is only relevant if you sell early. Smart conservative investors like Akshay hold to maturity and sleep soundly.

image.alt: Bond Prices, Yields, and Duration — Bonds, FDs & Fixed Income — Lending Your Money

slides.title: Credit Risk and Default

points.label: Credit Risk
points.text: Risk that the bond issuer (government or corporation) won't pay you back. Governments almost never default (backed by nation's assets). Corporations sometimes do—if a company goes bankrupt, its bonds may be worthless.

points.label: Credit Rating
points.text: Agencies like CRISIL, ICRA rate bond safety: AAA (safest, government-like), AA, A (medium-safe), BBB, BB (risky). A ₹100 bond rated BBB might offer 8% coupon to compensate for higher risk, while AAA rated bonds offer 5%.

points.label: Subordinated Bonds
points.text: If a corporation defaults, creditors are paid in order: first secured loans (backed by assets), then unsecured bonds, then subordinated bonds. Subordinated bonds carry highest risk.

example.problem: Akshay can invest ₹5 lakhs in: (A) Government G-Sec at 5.5% (AAA rating, zero default risk), or (B) Corporate Bond from a risky software startup at 8.5% (BB rating, 2% default probability). Which should he choose?
example.solution: For Akshay's ₹10L inheritance, A is better. Why? (B) has a 2% chance of losing ₹5L (catastrophic). (A) is guaranteed. Yes, Akshay foregoes ₹1,50,000 per year (3% extra × 5L), but the peace of mind and capital safety are worth it. Only after 2-3 generations of family wealth would one risk 2% of principal for 3% extra return.

slides.inSimpleWords: Safer bonds pay lower interest. Riskier bonds pay higher interest. Conservative investors like Akshay prefer lower interest with zero risk. Aggressive investors bet on risky corporations and chase high returns. Both approaches work; depends on your personality and time horizon.

image.alt: Credit Risk and Default — Bonds, FDs & Fixed Income — Lending Your Money

slides.title: The Ladder Strategy
slides.storyContext: Akshay tells Rahul: 'I want to invest ₹10 lakhs over 5 years, but I'm afraid I'll lock it all in 5-year FDs and then need money early. What should I do?' Rahul smiles: 'Ladder strategy. Invest ₹2 lakhs each in: 1-year FD, 2-year FD, 3-year FD, 4-year FD, 5-year FD. Every year, one matures. You have cash. If you don't need it, reinvest in a new 5-year FD. This way, you lock higher rates (5-year pays more than 1-year) and maintain liquidity. Best of both worlds.' Akshay: 'So after 5 years, ₹2L matures every year, and I can redeploy it?' Rahul: 'Exactly. You're building a perpetual income stream plus flexibility.'

image.alt: The Ladder Strategy — Bonds, FDs & Fixed Income — Lending Your Money

slides.title: Comparing All Fixed-Income Options: A 5-Year Horizon
slides.storyContext: Akshay has ₹5 lakhs to invest for 5 years. Ms. Gupta shows him the options.

example.problem: Option 1: Bank FD at 6.5% p.a. (₹5,00,000 × 6.5% × 5 = ₹1,62,500 interest). Option 2: NSC at 8% p.a. (compound, ₹5,00,000 → ₹7,35,991). Option 3: Government Bond at 6% p.a., buy at face value. Which is best?
example.solution: NSC: ₹7,35,991 (highest return, TAX-FREE). Bond: ₹5,00,000 + ₹1,50,000 (coupons) = ₹6,50,000 (no tax). FD: ₹6,62,500 (before tax; if Akshay's father pays 30% tax on ₹1,62,500 = ₹48,750 tax, net = ₹6,13,750). For Akshay (zero tax bracket), all three are similar after tax. But for his father, NSC is clearly best (no tax). The choice also depends on flexibility—FDs can be withdrawn early with penalty; NSC has fixed tenure.

slides.inSimpleWords: Bank FDs, NSC, and Government Bonds all keep your money safe. NSC and Government savings usually beat FDs because they're tax-free. If you're in a high tax bracket, this advantage is HUGE. If you're a student (zero tax), the difference is smaller.

slides.storyContext: Five years later, Akshay reviews his portfolio. His ₹1.5L in NSC grew to ₹2.2L (tax-free). His ₹5L in FDs grew to ₹6.6L (after tax: ₹6.1L). His ₹3.5L in G-Secs is now worth ₹3.5L + ₹1L in coupons collected (tax-free). Total: ₹10L → ₹12.3L (conservative estimate). No volatility, no panic, no sleepless nights. Akshay smiles: 'I'm not a billionaire, but I've got solid wealth. And I didn't have to watch the stock market every day.' Rahul nods: 'That's the power of boring, compounding wealth. Now, if you'd invested in stocks instead, you might have ₹15–18L or ₹8L (depending on luck). But you'd have stress. Which life do you prefer?'

slides.title: Challenge: Build a Fixed-Income Portfolio
slides.storyContext: Akshay's plan: invest ₹10 lakhs over the next 5 years. He wants to grow his wealth safely without worrying about stock market crashes. Design his portfolio.

points.text: How much should he allocate to 1-year FDs (liquid, lower returns)?
How much to 5-year FDs (higher returns, medium lock-in)?
How much to NSC or PPF (tax-free, very safe, long-term)?
What's his expected return after 5 years?

example.problem: Sample allocation: ₹2,00,000 in 1-year FD (for emergencies, 5.5%), ₹5,00,000 in 5-year FD (core, 6.5%), ₹3,00,000 in NSC (tax-free growth, 8%). Expected blended return ≈ (2L × 5.5% + 5L × 6.5% + 3L × 8%) ÷ 10L ≈ 6.7% p.a. Over 5 years: ₹10L → ₹13.7L (approximately). He more than doubled his money safely, with zero stock market risk.
example.solution: Any allocation is valid as long as Akshay understands the trade-off: liquid (1-year FD) gives lower returns but lets him access money quickly. Long-term (NSC, PPF) gives higher returns but locks money for years. A balanced mix of both ensures both growth and liquidity.

slides.title: Challenge: Compare Risk & Return
slides.storyContext: Akshay's friend Arjun (same age, same ₹10L inheritance) invests 100% in stocks. After 5 years: Arjun's portfolio is worth ₹16L (lucky, good market). Akshay's fixed-income portfolio is worth ₹13.7L. Arjun boasts: 'I made 60% returns! You only made 37%!' Akshay doesn't feel bad. Why?

points.text: What would Arjun's portfolio be worth if the market crashed 50% instead?
What's Akshay's portfolio worth in the same crash scenario?
Who sleeps better? Who has more financial security?
Over 20 years, compound growth: Akshay's 6.7% vs. Arjun's average 12% (but volatile)—who ends up richer?

example.problem: Answers:
example.solution: 1. Arjun's ₹16L → ₹8L (50% crash). 2. Akshay's ₹13.7L stays ₹13.7L (no crash). 3. Akshay wins on security. 4. Over 20 years: Akshay: ₹10L × (1.067)^20 ≈ ₹40L. Arjun (if averaging 12%): ₹10L × (1.12)^20 ≈ ₹96L. BUT if Arjun hits a crash in year 5-10, his recovery takes years. Akshay's steady compound growth is predictable. Both strategies work; it depends on risk tolerance and time horizon.

slides.title: What We Learned: Fixed-Income Investing

points.text: A bond is a loan you give to a government or corporation. You receive periodic interest (coupon) and get your principal back at maturity.
FDs let you deposit money in a bank for a fixed period at a guaranteed rate. They're insured up to ₹5 lakhs and are very safe.
Government savings schemes (NSC, PPF, G-Secs) are backed by India's government and often offer TAX-FREE returns. They're the safest investment.
Fixed-income returns (5–8%) are lower than stock returns (~12–15%), but fixed-income is PREDICTABLE and SAFE. You know exactly how much you'll have in 5 years.

If you hold a bond or FD to maturity, you're guaranteed your principal + interest. Selling early can lock in losses if rates rose, but most conservative investors hold to maturity and avoid this risk.
Credit rating (AAA vs. BBB) matters. Government bonds and bank FDs are safe. Corporate bonds carry default risk. Higher risk = higher interest rate.

slides.inSimpleWords: Stocks are exciting but risky—Reliance might 10x or go to zero. Bonds and FDs are boring but safe—you know exactly how much you'll earn. For building long-term wealth without worry, fixed-income is the foundation. Combine it with some stocks for growth, and you have a balanced life.
